ch38.anchor: billeted ahead and lodge at the honjin
ch38.note: A honjin was the official inn of a post-station on the great highways, reserved for daimyō, court nobles, and high shogunal officials on their journeys; quarters were booked ahead by billeting-men, and a wooden placard (sekifuda) naming the lodger was hung at the gate. For a farmer’s son to travel so, with a name-board of his own, is the whole comedy of the chapter’s opening.

ch38.anchor: the site of the Naval Drill Ground at Teppōzu
ch38.note: The signs of the opening country were rising in Edo itself: a school for training with foreigners by the Hitotsubashi gate, and, on the old naval ground at Teppōzu (Tsukiji), the Tsukiji Hotel, Japan’s first Western-style hotel, begun in 1867 for the foreign residents the treaties now admitted. Historically grounded.

The Kiheitai, ‘irregular militia,’ was the mixed-class volunteer corps raised in Chōshū by Takasugi Shinsaku in 1863, open to farmers and townsmen alongside samurai; drilled in Western style, it became the backbone of Chōshū’s new army. Toshizō wants the same raw material for the same reason — that men with a stipend to lose no longer fight.

An anpotsu-kago was a heavier, better-appointed palanquin than the open town kind, one that sumptuary custom reserved to samurai households of standing. That Toshizō arrives home in one is exactly the ‘stiff neck’ the Hino folk resent.

Ishida sanyaku, ‘Ishida Powder,’ was a real folk remedy for bruises and sprains compounded by the Hijikata family of Ishida village and hawked from village to village — the trade the boy Toshizō carried on his own back. Koryōsan, ‘consumption powder,’ was another family preparation; that it could do nothing for Okita’s tuberculosis makes Toshizō’s faith in it the more affecting.

ch38.anchor: returned the government to the throne
ch38.note: The Taisei Hōkan: on the fourteenth of the tenth month of Keiō 3 (9 November 1867) the shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu formally offered to return the governing power to the imperial Court, and it was accepted the next day — ending, on paper, two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule. Toshizō sets out to recruit for a shogunate that has, unknown to him, just surrendered its authority; the news reaches him only at Odawara. Historically exact.

The phrase renders nishiki o kazaru, ‘to deck oneself in brocade’ — from an old Chinese saying that to win success and not return home to be seen in it is like walking abroad by night in embroidered silk. Hikogorō means that Toshizō owes the home country the sight of his success; Toshizō, characteristically, will not perform it.
